## 1. PCA of UK food data

> First, we will import our data by reading the provided UK_foods.csv input file

```{r}

url <- "https://tinyurl.com/UK-foods"
x <- read.csv(url)
```

> **Q1.** How many rows and columns are in your new data frame named x? What R functions could you use to answer this question?

> **Answer:** There are 17 rows and 5 columns.

```{r}
# The nrow() function returns the number of rows
nrow(x)
# The ncol(x) function returns the number of columns
ncol(x)
# The dim() function returns the number of rows AND columns
dim(x)
```

> Second, we will check our imported data

```{r}
# The View() function displays all the data in a new tab in RStudio
# The head() function prints the first 6 rows of the dataset
# The tail() function prints the last 6 rows of the dataset
## Preview the first 6 rows
head(x)
```

> Correct the row names so that we have 4 columns not 5

```{r}
# The rownames() function sets row names for data frames
rownames(x) <- x[,1]
# A negative index removes elements
# Here, the -1 column index removes the first column
x <- x[,-1]
head(x)
```

> Check the dimensions again

```{r}
dim(x)
```

> Alternative approach to correcting row names

```{r}
# Read the data file and set the row.names argument of read.csv
# to be the first column
# (i.e. use argument setting row.names=1)
x <- read.csv(url, row.names=1)
head(x)
```

> **Q2.** Which approach to solving the 'row-names problem' mentioned above do you prefer and why? Is one approach more robust than another under certain circumstances?

> **Answer:** I prefer the second approach because it is faster and more robust than the first approach. If you run the first code (x \<- x\[,-1\]) more than once, you lose the first column every time the code is executed.

> Generate a bar plot using base R

```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=T, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))
```

> **Q3.** Changing what optional argument in the above barplot() function results in the following plot?

> **Answer:** Changing the beside argument from true to false should stack the bars.

```{r}
# The beside argument controls how multiple groups of data are displayed
# beside = TRUE creates a side-by-side (grouped) bar chart
# beside = FALSE creates a stacked bar chat
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=F, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))
```

> Tidying data

```{r}
# Install the package tidyr
# install.packages("tidyr")
# Load the package tidyr
library(tidyr)

# Convert data to long format for ggplot with 'pivot_longer()'
x_long <- x |> tibble::rownames_to_column("Food") |> pivot_longer(cols = -Food, 
names_to = "Country", values_to = "Consumption")
dim(x_long)
head(x_long)
```

> Generate a grouped barplot using ggplot

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(x_long) + aes(x = Country, y = Consumption, fill = Food) + 
geom_col(position = "dodge") + theme_bw()
```

> **Q4.** Changing what optional argument in the above ggplot() code results in a stacked barplot figure?

> **Answer:** Changing the position argument in the geom_col() function from dodge to stack stacks the bars.

```{r}
# The position argument in the geom_col() function controls how
# multiple groups of data are displayed similar to the beside argument
# position = "dodge" creates a side-by-side (grouped) bar chart
# position = "stack" creates a stacked bar chat
ggplot(x_long) + aes(x = Country, y = Consumption, fill = Food) + 
geom_col(position = "stack") + theme_bw()
```

> **Q5.** We can use the pairs() function to generate all pairwise plots for our countries. Can you make sense of the following code and resulting figure? What does it mean if a given point lies on the diagonal for a given plot?

> **Answer:** In the first row, England is the y axis for all plots. Wales is the x axis for the second plot, Scotland for the third, and N. Ireland for the fourth. If a given point lies on the diagonal, it means that equal amounts of food is being consumed by people from both countries.

```{r}
pairs(x, col=rainbow(nrow(x)), pch=16)
```

> Generate a heatmap

```{r}
# install.packages("pheatmap")
library(pheatmap)
pheatmap(as.matrix(x))
```

> **Q6.** Based on the pairs and heatmap figures, which countries cluster together and what does this suggest about their food consumption patterns? Can you easily tell what the main differences between N. Ireland and the other countries of the UK in terms of this dataset?

> **Answer:** England and Wales cluster closest together. This suggests that food consumption patterns in England, Wales, and Scotland are relatively similar to one another, with England and Wales having the most nearly identical dietary profile. It is difficult to tell specific differences between N. Ireland and the other countries because of the similar hues.

> PCA to the rescue

```{r}
# The prcomp() function performs Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on a given
# data matrix
# The t() function transposes a matrix or data frame (flipping its rows and
# columns)
pca <- prcomp(t(x))
summary(pca)
```

> **Q7.** Complete the code below to generate a plot of PC1 vs PC2. The second line adds text labels over the data points.

```{r}
# Create a data frame for plotting
df <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
df$Country <- rownames(df)

# Plot PC1 vs PC2 with ggplot
ggplot(pca$x) + aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, label=rownames(pca$x)) + geom_point(size=3) + 
geom_text(vjust=-0.5) + xlim(-270,500) + xlab("PC1") + 
ylab("PC2") + theme_bw()
```

> **Q8.** Customize your plot so that the colors of the country names match the colors in our UK and Ireland map and table at start of this document.

```{r}
# Create a vector that assigns colors to the countries in order (England, 
# Wales, Scotland, N. Ireland)
country_cols <- c("orange","red","blue","darkgreen")
# Plot PC1 vs PC2 with ggplot using color
# The color argument in the geom_text() function sets the text color
ggplot(pca$x) + aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, label=rownames(pca$x)) + geom_point(size=3) + 
geom_text(vjust=-0.5, col=country_cols) + xlim(-270,500) + xlab("PC1") + ylab("PC2") + theme_bw()
```

> Calculate how much variation in the original data each PC accounts for

```{r}
# pca$sdev returns the standard deviations of the principal components
# extracted during a PCA
# square pca$sdev to get the actual variance
v <- round(pca$sdev^2/sum(pca$sdev^2)*100)
v
```

```{r}
## or the second row here...
z <- summary(pca)
z$importance
```

> This information can be summarized in a plot of the variances (eigenvalues) with respect to the principal component number (eigenvector number), which is given below

```{r}
# Create scree plot with ggplot
variance_df <- data.frame(PC=factor(paste0("PC", 1:length(v)), 
levels=paste0("PC", 1:length(v))), Variance=v)

ggplot(variance_df) + aes(x=PC, y=Variance) + geom_col(fill="steelblue") + 
xlab("Principal Component") + ylab("Percent Variation") + theme_bw() + 
theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=0))
```

> We can also consider the influence of each of the original variables upon the principal components (typically known as loading scores).

```{r}
## Lets focus on PC1 as it accounts for > 90% of variance
ggplot(pca$rotation) + aes(x=PC1, y=reorder(rownames(pca$rotation), PC1)) + 
geom_col(fill="steelblue") + xlab("PC1 Loading Score") + ylab("") + 
theme_bw() + theme(axis.text.y=element_text(size=9))
```

> **Q9.** Generate a similar 'loadings plot' for PC2. What two food groups feature prominently and what does PC2 mainly tell us about?

> **Answer:** Fresh potatoes and soft drinks are the prominent food groups. PC2 separates countries based on their consumption of fresh potatoes vs soft drinks (driven largely by Scotland at the positive end of PC2 and Wales at the negative end of PC2)

```{r}
# Change the x-axis mapping from PC1 to PC2 so that the bar lengths represent 
# the loading scores for Principal Component 2
# Change the reordering variable inside the reorder() function from PC2 to PC2 
# so that the foods are sorted sequentially along the vertical axis 
# based on their PC2 values rather than PC1
# Changed the x-axis label from "PC1 Loading Score" to "PC2 Loading Score" to 
# accurately reflect the data being plotted
ggplot(pca$rotation) + aes(x=PC2, y=reorder(rownames(pca$rotation), PC2)) + 
geom_col(fill="steelblue") + xlab("PC2 Loading Score") + ylab("") + 
theme_bw() + theme(axis.text.y=element_text(size=9))
```

## 2. PCA of RNA-seq data

> First, we will import our data by reading the provided expression.csv input file

```{r}
url2 <- "https://tinyurl.com/expression-CSV"
rna.data <- read.csv(url2, row.names=1)
head(rna.data)
```

> **Q10.** How many genes and samples are in this data set? How many PCs do you think it will take to have a useful overview of this data set (see below).

> **Answer:** There are 100 genes and 11 samples. 2 PCAs are sufficient. In binary group setups, PC1 almost always captures the majority of variation, while PC2 captures any remaining secondary variation.

```{r}
# Genes are rows and samples are columns
# Use the dim() function to find the number of the rows AND columns
dim(rna.data)
```

> Generating barplots etc. to make sense of this data is really not an exciting or worthwhile option to consider. So lets do PCA and plot the results:

```{r}
## Again we have to take the transpose of our data
pca <- prcomp(t(rna.data), scale=TRUE)

# Create data frame for plotting
df <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
df$Sample <- rownames(df)

## Plot with ggplot
ggplot(df) + aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, label=Sample) + geom_point(size=3) + 
geom_text(vjust=-0.5, size=3) + xlab("PC1") + ylab("PC2") + theme_bw()
```

> Examine a summary of how much variation in the original data each PC accounts for

```{r}
summary(pca)
```

> A quick scree plot summary of this Proportion of Variance for each PC can be obtained using ggplot:

```{r}
# Calculate variance explained
pca.var <- pca$sdev^2
pca.var.per <- round(pca.var/sum(pca.var)*100,1)

# Create scree plot data
scree_df <- data.frame(PC=factor(paste0("PC", 1:10), levels=paste0("PC",1:10)), 
Variance=pca.var[1:10])

ggplot(scree_df) + aes(x=PC, y=Variance) + geom_col(fill="steelblue") + 
ggtitle("Quick scree plot") + xlab("Principal Component") + ylab("Variance") + theme_bw()
```

> Let's make another version showing percent variation:

```{r}
## Percent variance is often more informative to look at
pca.var.per
```

```{r}
# Create percent variance scree plot
scree_pct_df <- data.frame(PC=factor(paste0("PC", 1:10), 
levels=paste0("PC", 1:10)), PercentVariation=pca.var.per[1:10])

ggplot(scree_pct_df) + aes(x=PC, y=PercentVariation) + 
geom_col(fill="steelblue") + ggtitle("Scree Plot") + 
xlab("Principal Component") + ylab("Percent Variation") + theme_bw()
```

> Now lets make our own main PCA plot a bit more attractive and useful...

```{r}
## A vector of colors for wt and ko samples
colvec <- colnames(rna.data)
colvec[grep("wt", colvec)] <- "red"
colvec[grep("ko", colvec)] <- "blue"

# Add condition to data frame
df$condition <- substr(df$Sample, 1,2)
df$color <- colvec

ggplot(df) + aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, color=color, label=Sample) + 
geom_point(size=3) + geom_text(vjust=-0.5, hjust=0.5, show.legend = FALSE) + 
scale_color_identity() + xlab(paste0("PC1 (", pca.var.per[1], "%)")) + 
ylab(paste0("PC2 (", pca.var.per[2], "%)")) + theme_bw()
```

> Gene loadings: let’s find the top 10 measurements (genes) that contribute most to pc1 in either direction (+ or -).

```{r}
loading_scores <- pca$rotation[,1]

## Find the top 10 measurements (genes) that contribute most to PC1 in
# either direction (+ or -)
gene_scores <- abs(loading_scores)
gene_score_ranked <- sort(gene_scores, decreasing=TRUE)

## Show the names of the top 10 genes
top_10_genes <- names(gene_score_ranked[1:10])
top_10_genes
```
